subject: Culture
title: Feasts and Abundance
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Feasts and Abundance.

hook.text: A Roman banquet could last eight hours and include 20 courses. Excess was the point.

buildup.text: Feasts mark transitions: weddings, harvests, victories, religious holidays. They punctuate time.

discovery.text: Anthropologist Mary Douglas found meals have grammar. A feast is a sentence that says 'we celebrate.'

twist.text: Puritan settlers considered feasting sinful. Then they invented Thanksgiving—America's biggest feast.

climax.text: Abundance on the table signals safety, gratitude, and status all at once.

punchline.text: A feast isn't about the food. It's about the occasion.

quiz.question: Who described meals as having a grammar or structure?

details.summary: Feasting traditions — from Thanksgiving to Chinese banquets to Nigerian naming ceremonies — celebrate abundance and reinforce social hierarchies. The size of the feast signals the host's generosity and wealth.
details.whyItMatters: Feasts reveal how food becomes a tool of social power. The economics of celebration — who feeds whom, how much, and how elaborately — maps precisely onto cultural hierarchies.
takeaways: Feasting has been a social power display for thousands of years
Chinese banquet culture involves elaborate rules of hospitality
Medieval European feasts displayed political power through food

faq.question: Why is hosting a feast a form of power?
faq.answer: Providing abundant food demonstrates wealth, generosity, and social command. Medieval lords fed hundreds to show dominance. Potlatch ceremonies involved competitive generosity. Chinese banquets follow strict hosting obligations.

faq.question: How do feasts reinforce community?
faq.answer: Communal feasting creates shared experience, distributes resources (especially in subsistence societies), marks important transitions (weddings, births, harvests), and temporarily dissolves social barriers. Eating together triggers oxytocin release and social bonding.
